fisher_checklist.criterion: Sufficient market potential for years of growth
fisher_checklist.evidence: Commercial remaining performance obligation increased 84% to $678 billion and Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 41%, with the filing describing ongoing expansion of datacenter capacity to meet 'growing demand for AI services,' suggesting a large and still-expanding addressable market.
R&D expenses increased 9% to $35.6 billion (11% of revenue), described as funding 'compute capacity, AI talent, and data to support product development that benefits the entire portfolio.'

Microsoft 365 Commercial seats grew 6% 'driven by small and medium businesses and frontline worker offerings,' and the filing details growth across commercial, consumer, and advertising channels across three segments.
Scorecard shows ROIC of 22.7% and FCF margin of 20.2%, both well above the stated thresholds (12% and 10% respectively), indicating genuinely strong profitability.

fisher_checklist.criterion: Steps to sustain or improve margin
fisher_checklist.evidence: The filing notes gross margin percentage decreased due to AI infrastructure investment but was 'offset in part by efficiency gains across the Microsoft Cloud' and in Azure/Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud specifically, indicating active efficiency initiatives alongside continued investment.

The excerpts mention competing for talent via 'exceptional working environment' and 'competitive compensation and benefits' but provide no substantive detail on actual labor relations, turnover, or employee sentiment.

fisher_checklist.criterion: Depth of management beyond the top executive
fisher_checklist.evidence: The excerpts reference an 'Information about our Executive Officers' section but the actual content is not provided, so no assessment of management bench depth can be made from this text.

The MD&A attributes margin changes generically to 'efficiency gains' and investment levels but does not describe specific cost-accounting systems or control processes beyond this high-level narrative.

fisher_checklist.criterion: A unique aspect giving a real competitive edge
fisher_checklist.evidence: Microsoft describes a long-term strategic partnership with OpenAI, stating it 'holds rights to OpenAI's intellectual property, including models and infrastructure, for integration into our products,' a specific, hard-to-replicate arrangement.

Management explicitly accepts that 'investments we are making in cloud and AI infrastructure...will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins,' framing near-term margin compression as a trade-off for longer-term positioning.

fisher_checklist.criterion: Equity financing that would dilute current shareholders
fisher_checklist.evidence: The liquidity section lists share repurchases (alongside dividends and debt maturities) as planned uses of cash, suggesting shares outstanding are being reduced rather than growth being funded via new equity issuance, though exact share count trends are not shown in these excerpts.

fisher_checklist.criterion: Management talks candidly about problems, not just successes
fisher_checklist.evidence: The filing specifically discloses a $28.9 billion IRS tax dispute, declining XBOX revenue with impairment charges, and margin percentage declines tied to AI infrastructure spend, rather than only generic risk boilerplate.

qualitative.management_assessment: The excerpts show management continuing to invest heavily in AI/cloud infrastructure and R&D (R&D up 9% to $35.6B, 11% of revenue) even as this compresses gross margin percentage, which the filing frames as a deliberate trade-off for future growth (e.g., Azure demand, AI product usage) rather than short-term margin optimization. The scorecard's very low debt/EBITDA (0.66x) and strong ROIC (22.7%) are consistent with conservative balance-sheet management, and the liquidity section references dividends, share repurchases, and debt maturities as planned uses of cash, though specific buyback/dividend figures are not included in these excerpts. Management also disclosed a major, unusual capital-allocation commitment—the extended OpenAI partnership and associated equity-method investment—which materially swung reported net income and EPS in both directions across the two years shown, indicating this is a significant and somewhat volatile strategic bet rather than routine capital deployment.
qualitative.moat_explanation: The excerpts describe commercial remaining performance obligation growing 84% to $678 billion, indicating large multi-year contracts, and Microsoft 365 Commercial seat growth (6%) tied to a suite of interlocking cloud products (Teams, SharePoint, Exchange, Copilot, Power BI) that make migration costly and disruptive for enterprise customers. This embedded, multi-product enterprise footprint is the strongest and most concretely evidenced competitive advantage in the text, more so than a specific network-effect, brand, or cost-advantage claim.
red_flags: IRS has proposed an additional $28.9 billion tax payment (plus penalties and interest) related to transfer pricing for tax years 2004-2013, which management is contesting
Gross margin percentage and Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage both declined due to continued AI infrastructure investment, acknowledged directly by the company as margin pressure
XBOX content and services revenue declined 5% and XBOX hardware revenue declined 29%, with impairment and other related expenses recorded in the XBOX business

Net income and diluted EPS were materially affected in both directions (positively in FY2026, negatively in FY2025) by mark-to-market style gains/losses on the OpenAI investment, adding earnings volatility tied to a single strategic relationship

Datacenter buildout depends on availability of permitted/buildable land, predictable energy, networking supplies, and components (including GPUs) from a limited pool of qualified suppliers, a constraint the company itself flags

falsification_criteria: If Microsoft's actual reported ROIC falls below the 12% threshold used in this scorecard in a subsequent 10-K, the quant pillar of the thesis would no longer hold as described

If commercial remaining performance obligation growth reverses or Microsoft 365 Commercial seat growth turns negative for multiple consecutive quarters, the switching-costs moat evidence cited here would be undermined

If the stock price falls enough that the DCF-implied margin of safety turns positive (i.e., price moves below the ~$235/share intrinsic estimate) or if updated DCF assumptions produce a materially different figure, the valuation objection in this thesis would be resolved

If the IRS $28.9 billion transfer-pricing dispute is resolved against Microsoft with a material cash payment recorded, that would confirm the red flag noted in the qualitative layer as a realized risk rather than a contingent one

If gross margin or Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage continues declining for several more reporting periods without offsetting efficiency gains, the 'deliberate trade-off' framing of management's AI spending would be called into question
If the OpenAI-related mark-to-market gains/losses produce a large negative swing to net income in a future period, the earnings volatility risk flagged in the qualitative layer would be substantiated
thesis.thesis: Microsoft's quant scorecard is essentially flawless (100% pass rate, 22.7% ROIC, 20.2% FCF margin, 14.6% revenue CAGR, low leverage), and the qualitative layer grounds this in a concrete, evidenced moat: switching costs from an interlocking enterprise product suite and $678B of commercial remaining performance obligations, reinforced by heavy R&D reinvestment and a unique OpenAI IP arrangement that Fisher-style analysis rates favorably across most criteria. However, the valuation layer cuts directly against this strong business narrative - the simplified two-stage DCF implies the current price is roughly 52% above the estimated intrinsic value per share, a substantial negative margin of safety, even though relative multiples (P/E and EV/EBITDA) sit modestly below sector medians. This is a case where quant and qualitative layers agree the business is excellent, but the DCF layer flags the price as demanding relative to that quality, so the three layers point in different directions rather than converging on a clean buy or avoid signal; a great business bought at a price the DCF finds excessive is not automatically a bargain just because peers are also expensive. Readers should weigh that the DCF's growth and discount-rate assumptions are simplified and sensitive, while also noting the filing-disclosed red flags (a $28.9B IRS tax dispute, margin compression from AI infrastructure spend, and earnings volatility tied to the OpenAI equity stake) as real, checkable risks to the moat and management story.
